Fresh Earth is revolutionizing the $13.4 trillion (2023) agri-food market.
Fresh Earth aims to create a global, community-based food system.
Fresh Earth empowers people to take control of their health, food quality, and food sources.
Fresh Earth includes a B2B marketplace that connects regenerative farmers with businesses.
Fresh Earth includes a B2C marketplace that encourages innovation and collaboration among stakeholders.
Fresh Earth includes a Project Management Platform.
Fresh Earth includes a Data Managment Platform that uses data to measure and validate the impact of regenerative practices.
Fresh Earth Token represents fractional ownership of the ecosystem.
Fresh Earth Token is valued based on the assets of the ecosystem and the impact of regenerative projects.
Fresh Earth creates a positive feedback loop where ecosystem success drives more investment, leading to more impact and greater value for token holders.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem is a decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) that manages the food ecosystem business.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem is designed to incentivize participation and engagement through different Incentive Drivers.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem includes a Rewards System.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem aims to empower individuals and businesses to take control of their food sources.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem aims to improve the quality and nutritional density of the food people consume.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem promotes sustainable practices and addresses climate change, health, and food security.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem aims to address climate change, health, and food security by promoting regenerative agriculture practices.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem aims to create a comprehensive, community-based food system.
The Fresh Earth ecosystem aims to regenerate the environment while improving food quality and nutritional density.
The token purpose and goals are to create a sustainable and regenerative food system.
The token purpose and goals include supporting farmers and communities.
The token purpose and goals include aligning incentives for token holders and ecosystem growth.
The token classification is described as a utility token and ERC-20 or other relevant classification.
Industrial agriculture is described as a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation, pollution, biodiversity loss, and decline in soil health and water availability.
Industrial agriculture is described as resulting in reduced crop yields and increased food insecurity.
The agri-food industry is described as facing health challenges due to soil degradation and chemical inputs.
Soil degradation and chemical inputs are described as leading to a decrease in nutritional density of food and an increase in food-borne illnesses and food toxicity.
The current industrial agriculture system is described as heavily reliant on fossil fuels.
The current industrial agriculture system is described as contributing to air and water pollution and negatively impacting the health of farmers and rural communities.
The current food system is described as inadequate in addressing food security issues.
Around 33% of global food production is described as lost or wasted.
Around 800 million people are described as suffering from hunger and malnutrition.
Consumers are described as becoming aware of environmental and health problems and demanding high-quality, sustainably produced food.
The market for organic and functional food is described as growing rapidly.
There is described to be a growing movement toward regenerative agriculture practices.
Regenerative agriculture practices are described as focusing on regenerating soil health, water availability, and biodiversity while producing food sustainably.

A lack of coordination and fragmentation in the agricultural industry is described as making it difficult for small farmers and regenerative agriculture projects to access capital to transition and scale up operations.
The current economic system is described as failing to account for the true cost of industrial agriculture on the environment and human health.

Farmers who want to grow crops using sustainable methods are described as investing in the transition and then being outcompeted by industrial practices that have not internalised their true costs to environment and health.
Unsustainable practices described include monoculture and heavy use of chemical inputs that degrade soil, reduce biodiversity, and increase greenhouse gas emissions and pollution.
Externalised costs are described as being subsidised by individuals in society who bear the cost of damages to environment and health.
On a true free market basis with all costs accounted for, regenerative and degenerative methods are described as competing on an equal basis.
Degenerative methods are described as having a burden of environmental, health, and expensive inputs costs such as fertiliser and pesticides.
Regenerative products are described as potentially becoming cheaper when regeneration is valued.
The monetary system is described as being based on fractional reserve banking and debt-based money creation.
The monetary system is described as exacerbating the problem by creating a cycle of debt repayment.
Most money is described as being created by commercial banks originating loans described as “Promises to Repay”.
Loan creation is described as creating an increase in deposit accounts described as “Money”.
The cycle of loan repayment is described as needing to come from commerce, predominately based on fossil fuel energy.
Because there is no accounting for natural capital, the ultimate source of repayment is described as a reduction in natural capital assets, i.e. destruction of environmental and health assets.
IMF loans to third world countries are described as making countries permanently indebted and required to mine natural capital, even food, to pay interest.
Greenhouse gas damage is described as only a fraction of the total environmental and health cost of the commerce system.

As long as destruction of nature is free of cost and money is debt based without regard to social value, the competitive race to the bottom is described as ensuring nature and health are destroyed faster.
The degenerative industrial agriculture industry is described as facing challenges that threaten global food security, economic stability, and human health.
Economic impact of food insecurity is described as up to 2% of GDP in developing countries due to micronutrient deficiencies according to Global Hunger Index 2014.
Global loss in economic productivity due to macronutrient and micronutrient deficiencies is described as over 2-3% of GDP.
The total cost of climate change is described as around 2-4% of global GDP by 2100 according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
Greenhouse gas emissions from the food sector are described as around 25% of global emissions.
Externalized damages of the $1T US food industry are described as estimated at $2.1T in a 2021 Rockefeller Report.
Annual healthcare costs globally due to diet-related chronic diseases are described as estimated by the World Health Organization at $2 trillion.
Deforestation caused by industrial agriculture is described as costing around $2-5 trillion annually in lost ecosystem services.
Loss of biodiversity caused by industrial agriculture is described as costing around $500 billion annually.
The use of chemical inputs in industrial agriculture is described as costing around $5.2 billion annually in health costs in the US alone.
Water pollution caused by agricultural activities is described as costing around $452 billion annually.
In a $100 trillion global GDP, these estimated costs are described as aggregating to $11-17 trillion.
